answers.plain:
The status code is the last field on each line, so this works:

```bash
awk '{c[$NF]++} END {for (s in c) print s, c[s]}' access.log
```

Replace `access.log` with your file path. With your sample lines, it prints something like this (`for (s in c)` doesn't guarantee an order):

```
200 2
404 1
500 1
```

To sort by status code, add `| sort`. To sort by count with the most frequent first, use `| sort -k2 -nr`.

Your examples show the lines separated by `|`. If your real log has one request per line, which is how access logs normally look, the command works as is. If everything is on a single line separated by `|`, use this instead:

```bash
tr '|' '\n' < access.log | awk 'NF {c[$NF]++} END {for (s in c) print s, c[s]}'
```

If your real log is the standard Apache or Nginx format, the status code isn't the last field. It's followed by the response size, so use `$9` instead of `$NF`. The standard format also has a quoted request such as `"GET /index HTTP/1.1"`.
answers.nudge:
```bash
awk '$NF ~ /^[1-5][0-9][0-9]$/ {c[$NF]++} END {for (s in c) printf "%s %d\n", s, c[s]}' access.log | sort -n
```

On your sample lines, it prints:

```
200 2
404 1
500 1
```

- **Status field:** In your format the status is the last field, so `$NF` picks it out.
- **Validation:** The `$NF ~ /^[1-5][0-9][0-9]$/` filter skips blank, truncated or garbled lines. Otherwise they would show up as bogus "status codes".
- **Sorting:** `sort -n` orders the output by status code. To rank by count, use `sort -k2,2nr` instead.
- **Input:** It works on a pipe too, for example `zcat access.log.gz | awk ...` or `tail -f`-style snapshots.

**Variations**
- **Shorter, no awk:** `grep -oE ' [1-5][0-9]{2}$' access.log | sort | uniq -c`. This prints the count first.
- **Standard Apache/Nginx combined format:** The request is quoted and the status is followed by a byte count, so use `$9` instead of `$NF`: `awk '{c[$9]++} END {for (s in c) print s, c[s]}' access.log | sort -n`.
- **Status classes only (2xx, 4xx, 5xx):** `awk '$NF ~ /^[1-5][0-9][0-9]$/ {c[substr($NF,1,1) "xx"]++} END {for (s in c) print s, c[s]}' access.log | sort`.

I assumed the ` | ` in your examples just separates lines for display. If the log really has several entries on one line, split them first with `tr '|' '\n' < access.log | awk ...`.
answers.skill:
The status code is the last field on each line, so:

```bash
awk '{print $NF}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

This prints each status code with its count, most frequent first, like `2 200`.

If you want the code first, then the count:

```bash
awk '{c[$NF]++} END {for (s in c) print s, c[s]}' access.log | sort
```

Notes:
- `$NF` is the last whitespace-separated field. Your sample lines end with the status code, so this works.
- Your examples were separated by `|`. If that's how the log really looks, with everything on one line, use this instead:
  ```bash
  grep -oE ' [1-5][0-9]{2}( \||$)' access.log | tr -dc '0-9\n' | sort | uniq -c
  ```
- If your real log is standard Apache/Nginx combined format, the status is field 9, so use `$9` instead of `$NF`.
